nodes.label: Sets, Subsets, and Elementary Set Algebra
nodes.explanation: Assumes university entry background in logic and proof methods (propositional connectives, quantifiers, direct proof, contraposition, contradiction, counterexamples, and biconditional proofs) together with familiarity with standard number systems ℕ, ℤ, ℚ, and ℝ. Introduces sets via roster and set-builder notation, membership (∈) versus subset inclusion (⊆ and proper subset ⊊), the empty set ∅ (proving ∅ ⊆ A vacuously and sharply distinguishing ∅ from {∅}), and set equality by extensionality (proving A = B via double inclusion A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A). Defines union (∪), intersection (∩), set difference (A \ B), symmetric difference (A Δ B), and complement (A^c relative to a fixed ambient universe), and develops element-chasing proofs of core Boolean set identities—distributivity, De Morgan's laws, absorption, and equivalence characterizations such as A ⊆ B ⇔ A ∩ B = A ⇔ A \ B = ∅ ⇔ B^c ⊆ A^c. Uses Venn diagrams purely as an intuition and counterexample-generation aid while establishing why diagrams do not constitute general proofs. Enables the learner to write rigorous element-chasing proofs and construct small finite counterexamples to false set identities. Leaves power sets, Cartesian products, arbitrary indexed families, and axiomatic set theory (ZFC) to later lessons or courses.

nodes.label: Power Sets and Cartesian Products
nodes.explanation: Builds on sets, subsets, and element-chasing set algebra to construct higher-order sets and ordered tuples. Defines the power set P(A) = {S : S ⊆ A}, carefully navigating the level distinction between ∈ and ⊆ (such as x ∈ A ⇔ {x} ⊆ A ⇔ {x} ∈ P(A), and P(∅) = {∅} ≠ ∅), proving A ⊆ B ⇔ P(A) ⊆ P(B) and P(A ∩ B) = P(A) ∩ P(B), and refuting P(A ∪ B) = P(A) ∪ P(B) via a concrete counterexample. Defines ordered pairs (a, b) via their characterizing equality property ((a, b) = (c, d) ⇔ a = c ∧ b = d, optionally noting Kuratowski's encoding {{a}, {a, b}} only as motivation without requiring axiomatic development) and the Cartesian product A × B (and finite n-tuples A₁ × ··· × A_n). Proves product-algebra identities such as A × (B ∪ C) = (A × B) ∪ (A × C), A × (B ∩ C) = (A × B) ∩ (A × C), and (A × B) ∩ (C × D) = (A ∩ C) × (B ∩ D), while diagnosing edge cases when a factor is empty (A × B = ∅ ⇔ A = ∅ ∨ B = ∅) and why (A × B) ∪ (C × D) ≠ (A ∪ C) × (B ∪ D) in general. Enables the learner to prove and refute identities involving power sets and Cartesian products cleanly. Leaves finite counting formulas like |P(A)| = 2^n to combinatorics and leaves binary relations and functions to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Indexed Families, Arbitrary Unions, and Intersections
nodes.explanation: Builds on sets, subsets, and element-chasing set algebra to extend union and intersection from finitely many sets to arbitrary indexed families {A_i}_{i ∈ I} where I may be finite, countably infinite, or uncountable. Translates arbitrary union ⋃_{i∈I} A_i = {x : ∃i ∈ I, x ∈ A_i} and arbitrary intersection ⋂_{i∈I} A_i = {x : ∀i ∈ I, x ∈ A_i} directly into existential and universal quantifiers, training element-chasing proofs of generalized De Morgan's laws ((⋃_{i∈I} A_i)^c = ⋂_{i∈I} A_i^c and dual) and generalized distributivity (B ∩ (⋃_{i∈I} A_i) = ⋃_{i∈I} (B ∩ A_i) and dual) using quantifier negation and distribution. Evaluates concrete infinite families of real intervals (such as ⋂_{n=1}^∞ (−1/n, 1/n) = {0}, ⋂_{n=1}^∞ (0, 1/n) = ∅, and ⋃_{n=1}^∞ [1/n, 1 − 1/n] = (0, 1)) to build intuition for how boundary points behave under infinite operations, and explicitly addresses the convention for an empty index set I = ∅ (empty union is ∅; empty intersection inside a universe U is U). Enables the learner to compute infinite unions and intersections rigorously and prove generalized set identities. Leaves formal functions and preimage identities to later lessons.

nodes.label: Binary Relations, Representations, and Properties
nodes.explanation: Builds on Cartesian products to formalize binary relations from A to B as subsets R ⊆ A × B, with primary focus on relations on a set A (R ⊆ A × A). Connects abstract set-of-pairs definitions with concrete representations—directed graphs and Boolean adjacency matrices on finite sets, and algebraic/divisibility/geometric relations on ℤ, ℝ, and P(X)—and introduces the inverse relation R^{-1} and relation composition S ∘ R. Develops rigorous tests and proof/counterexample strategies for the five central properties on A: reflexivity, irreflexivity, symmetry, antisymmetry, and transitivity. Directly confronts persistent misconceptions: symmetry and antisymmetry are neither logical opposites nor mutually exclusive (the equality relation is both; many relations are neither), and antisymmetry or transitivity can hold vacuously when no qualifying pairs exist. Enables the learner to classify binary relations on finite and infinite sets, verify or refute each structural property with precision, and compute inverses and compositions of relations. Leaves equivalence relations, partial orders, and functions to separate specialized branches.

nodes.label: Equivalence Relations and Equivalence Classes
nodes.explanation: Builds on binary relations and their properties to study equivalence relations—relations on A that are reflexive, symmetric, and transitive—as the mathematical mechanism for identifying objects that share an invariant. Works through canonical examples across mathematics: congruence modulo n on ℤ, same-parity or same-remainder relations, similarity/parallelism in geometry, and the fraction-construction relation (a, b) ∼ (c, d) ⇔ ad = bc on ℤ × (ℤ \ {0}). Defines equivalence classes [a] = {x ∈ A : x ∼ a} and proves the Fundamental Lemma of Equivalence Classes: (1) a ∈ [a], (2) a ∼ b ⇔ [a] = [b], and (3) for any a, b ∈ A, either [a] = [b] or [a] ∩ [b] = ∅. Introduces well-definedness of operations on equivalence classes (proving that [a] + [b] = [a + b] and [a][b] = [ab] in ℤ/nℤ are independent of choice of representatives, contrasted with an ill-defined rule such as [a] ↦ a mod m when m does not divide n). Enables the learner to verify equivalence relations, describe equivalence classes explicitly, and test well-definedness on classes. Leaves partitions and the global correspondence with quotient sets to the next lesson.

nodes.label: Partitions, Quotient Sets, and the Fundamental Correspondence
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes indexed families of sets with equivalence relations and equivalence classes to establish the global structural correspondence between equivalence relations and partitions. Defines a partition of a set A as a collection P of nonempty, pairwise disjoint subsets of A whose union is A, and defines the quotient set A/∼ = {[a] : a ∈ A} of all equivalence classes. Proves the Fundamental Theorem of Equivalence Relations: every equivalence relation ∼ on A yields a partition A/∼ of A; conversely, every partition P of A defines an equivalence relation (x ∼_P y iff x and y belong to the same block of P); and these two constructions are exact mutual inverses (the equivalence classes of ∼_P recover P, and the relation induced by A/∼ recovers ∼). Applies this correspondence to translate between classifying elements by invariants, decomposing domains into disjoint fibers, and designing equivalence relations with prescribed classes. Enables the learner to verify partitions, construct quotient sets, and move freely between equivalence relations and partitions. Leaves canonical factorization of general functions through quotient sets to an optional enrichment lesson.

nodes.label: Partial Orders, Total Orders, and Hasse Diagrams
nodes.explanation: Builds on binary relations and their properties to develop partial orders—relations on P that are reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive—and strict partial orders (<, irreflexive and transitive, showing the canonical correspondence x < y ⇔ (x ≤ y ∧ x ≠ y)). Investigates core posets (P, ≤) across different domains: standard ordering on ℝ, divisibility (ℤ^+, |), subset inclusion (P(X), ⊆), and product and lexicographic orders on P × Q. Distinguishes total (linear) orders (where all pairs are comparable) from partial orders with incomparable elements, and introduces chains (totally ordered subsets) and antichains (pairwise incomparable subsets). Develops cover relations (y covers x when x < y with no z strictly between them) to construct and read Hasse diagrams for finite posets, verifying how transitivity and reflexivity are omitted visually while remaining part of the relation. Enables the learner to verify partial and total orders, compare product and lexicographic orderings, and translate fluently between finite posets and Hasse diagrams. Leaves extremal elements, bounds, suprema, and well-ordering to the next lesson.

nodes.label: Extremal Elements, Bounds, Suprema, and Well-Ordering
nodes.explanation: Builds on partial orders, total orders, and Hasse diagrams to analyze distinguished elements and order completeness properties inside posets. Sharpens the crucial distinction between minimal/maximal elements (no strictly smaller/larger element exists) and least/greatest elements (comparable to and below/above every element), proving that least and greatest elements are unique if they exist and that every least element is the unique minimal element, while exhibiting finite and infinite posets with multiple minimal elements or none at all. Defines upper and lower bounds of a subset S ⊆ P, least upper bound (supremum / join, sup S), and greatest lower bound (infimum / meet, inf S), proving uniqueness of sup and inf when they exist and interpreting them concretely in (P(X), ⊆) (union and intersection), (ℤ^+, |) (lcm and gcd), and (ℚ, ≤) versus (ℝ, ≤). Introduces well-ordered sets (total orders in which every nonempty subset has a least element), contrasting (ℕ, ≤) and lexicographic ℕ × ℕ with (ℤ, ≤), (ℚ^+, ≤), and ([0, 1], ≤). Enables the learner to locate extremal elements, bounds, suprema, and infima in arbitrary posets and test whether an order is a well-ordering. Leaves Zorn's Lemma, transfinite induction, and lattice homomorphisms outside the core path.

nodes.label: Functions as Relations, Domains, and Codomains
nodes.explanation: Builds on binary relations (with informal prior familiarity with algebraic formulas from school mathematics) to establish the rigorous set-theoretic definition of a function. Defines a function f : A → B as a relation f ⊆ A × B satisfying existence and uniqueness (∀a ∈ A, ∃!b ∈ B, (a, b) ∈ f), specifying f cleanly by its domain A, codomain B, and rule/graph, and defines function equality (f = g iff they have the same domain, the same codomain, and f(a) = g(a) for all a ∈ A—emphasizing why changing the codomain alters the function even when the formula is unchanged). Distinguishes codomain from range (image im(f)), tests whether proposed rules are well-defined (checking domain coverage, target membership, consistency at overlaps in piecewise rules, and independence of representation such as reduced vs. unreduced fractions p/q), and introduces identity maps, inclusion maps, restrictions f|_S, extensions, and indicator (characteristic) functions χ_S : X → {0, 1}. Enables the learner to verify well-definedness of functions, test function equality rigorously, and distinguish functions from general relations. Leaves direct images/preimages of subsets and injectivity/surjectivity to the next lessons.

nodes.label: Direct Images and Preimages of Sets
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes indexed families of sets with the formal definition of functions to develop the induced set-valued operations of direct image f(S) = {f(x) : x ∈ S} (for S ⊆ A) and preimage (inverse image) f^{-1}(T) = {x ∈ A : f(x) ∈ T} (for T ⊆ B). Confronts the central notational misconception directly: f^{-1}(T) is defined for every function f and every subset T ⊆ B regardless of whether f is invertible, whereas f^{-1}(y) as an element requires an inverse function. Proves the exact algebraic behavior of preimages and images over arbitrary indexed families by element chasing: preimages preserve arbitrary unions, arbitrary intersections, set differences, and complements without any hypotheses on f; direct images preserve arbitrary unions (f(⋃ S_i) = ⋃ f(S_i)) but satisfy only one-sided inclusions f(⋂ S_i) ⊆ ⋂ f(S_i), S ⊆ f^{-1}(f(S)), and f(f^{-1}(T)) ⊆ T in general, paired with concrete counterexamples where strict inclusion occurs. Enables the learner to compute images and preimages for algebraic and finite maps and prove or refute set-image identities accurately. Leaves characterizing equality in these inclusions via injectivity and surjectivity to the next lesson.

nodes.label: Injectivity, Surjectivity, and Bijections
nodes.explanation: Builds on direct images and preimages to develop the three core structural properties of mappings: injectivity (one-to-one: f(x₁) = f(x₂) ⇒ x₁ = x₂, or contrapositive), surjectivity (onto: ∀y ∈ B, ∃x ∈ A, f(x) = y, equivalently im(f) = B), and bijectivity (both injective and surjective). Trains proof and disproof templates across algebraic, piecewise, modular, tuple, and set-valued functions—including the two-part surjectivity check (solving f(x) = y for x in terms of y AND verifying x ∈ A) and illustrating how restricting domain or shrinking codomain alters injectivity or surjectivity. Connects injectivity and surjectivity directly back to set-image identities from the prior lesson: proves that f is injective iff f^{-1}(f(S)) = S for all S ⊆ A iff f(S₁ ∩ S₂) = f(S₁) ∩ f(S₂) for all S₁, S₂ ⊆ A, and that f is surjective iff f(f^{-1}(T)) = T for all T ⊆ B. Enables the learner to prove or refute injectivity, surjectivity, and bijectivity rigorously and translate them into preimage/image characterizations. Leaves composition, inverses, and infinite cardinality comparisons to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Function Composition and Left, Right, and Two-Sided Inverses
nodes.explanation: Builds on injectivity, surjectivity, and bijections to analyze function composition (g ∘ f : A → C defined when codomain(f) = domain(g)) and invertibility. Proves associativity of composition (h ∘ (g ∘ f) = (h ∘ g) ∘ f) and non-commutativity, and establishes how injectivity and surjectivity interact with composition: compositions of injections/surjections/bijections retain those properties; if g ∘ f is injective then f is injective (with a concrete counterexample where g is not injective); and if g ∘ f is surjective then g is surjective (with a concrete counterexample where f is not surjective). Proves the fundamental characterization of two-sided inverses: f : A → B has a two-sided inverse g : B → A (g ∘ f = id_A and f ∘ g = id_B) if and only if f is bijective, in which case the inverse f^{-1} is unique and satisfies (g ∘ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} ∘ g^{-1}. Develops one-sided inverses for nonempty A: f is injective iff it has a left inverse, and f is surjective iff it has a right inverse (explicitly noting that selecting one preimage per nonempty fiber relies on a choice principle for arbitrary infinite sets, while constructing explicit left/right inverses on concrete domains). Enables the learner to deduce properties of factors from compositions and construct or prove nonexistence of left, right, and two-sided inverses. Leaves cardinality theory to the next lessons.

nodes.label: Equinumerosity, Finite Sets, and Countable Sets
nodes.explanation: Builds on function composition and inverse functions to launch cardinality theory via bijections. Defines equinumerosity (|A| = |B| iff there exists a bijection A → B) and proves reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity of equinumerosity using identity maps, inverses, and compositions. Defines finite sets (empty or equinumerous with {1, ..., n} for some n ∈ ℕ, explicitly supplying uniqueness of n and basic finite-subset strictness without developing a full induction or combinatorics unit) and infinite sets, contrasting finite behavior with infinite sets that admit bijections onto proper subsets (Hilbert's Hotel shift maps on ℕ). Defines countably infinite and countable (finite or countably infinite) sets, proving that every subset of ℕ is countable and constructing explicit bijections or surjections from ℕ to prove countability of ℤ, ℕ × ℕ (via diagonal/pairing enumeration or prime-power encoding), ℚ, and countable unions of countable sets (noting explicitly where countable choice enters when choosing enumerations for arbitrary families). Enables the learner to prove equinumerosity via explicit bijections and prove countability of structured sets such as polynomials with rational coefficients or finite binary strings. Leaves uncountability, Cantor's Theorem, and Schröder–Bernstein to the next lessons.

nodes.label: Uncountability, Cantor's Diagonal Argument, and Cantor's Theorem
nodes.explanation: Builds on equinumerosity and countable sets to prove that infinite sets come in strictly different sizes. Develops Cantor's diagonal argument first on the set {0, 1}^ℕ of infinite binary sequences (where representation is unique and the diagonal flip is completely transparent), then adapts it to prove that the open interval (0, 1)—and hence ℝ, via an explicit bijection such as x ↦ tan(π(x − 1/2)) or a piecewise-rational map—is uncountable, carefully eliminating the non-uniqueness trap of repeating 9s (e.g., constructing the diagonal decimal using only digits 3 and 7). Proves Cantor's Theorem in full generality: for every set A, there is no surjection f : A → P(A), by constructing the diagonal subset D = {a ∈ A : a ∉ f(a)} and deriving the contradiction a_0 ∈ D ⇔ a_0 ∉ D if f(a_0) = D. Deduces an endless hierarchy of strictly larger cardinalities (|ℕ| < |P(ℕ)| < |P(P(ℕ))| < ···) and briefly notes why Russell's paradox forbids a "set of all sets". Enables the learner to execute diagonalization arguments cleanly and prove uncountability of concrete sets. Leaves formal cardinal comparison via injections and the Schröder–Bernstein Theorem to the culminating lesson.

nodes.label: Cardinal Comparison and the Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein Theorem
nodes.explanation: Builds on uncountability and Cantor's Theorem (using composition, inverses, and indexed unions from earlier ancestors) to establish the rigorous toolkit for comparing arbitrary cardinalities without building awkward explicit bijections. Defines |A| ≤ |B| via existence of an injection A → B (and strict inequality |A| < |B| via |A| ≤ |B| and |A| ≠ |B|, verifying equivalence with existence of a surjection B → A when A ≠ ∅, noting the choice principle if invoked) and verifies reflexivity and transitivity of ≤. Proves the Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein Theorem—if there exist injections f : A → B and g : B → A, then there exists a bijection h : A → B—via the clean iterative-union construction C = ⋃_{n=0}^∞ (g ∘ f)^n(A \ g(B)) (defining h(x) = f(x) for x ∈ C and h(x) = g^{-1}(x) for x ∈ A \ C, verifying every step of well-definedness, injectivity, and surjectivity without handwaving infinite backtracking chains). Applies Schröder–Bernstein together with earlier results to prove effortlessly that |(0, 1)| = |[0, 1]| = |ℝ| = |{0, 1}^ℕ| = |P(ℕ)| = |ℝ × ℝ| (via digit interleaving). Enables the learner to prove equinumerosity of infinite sets by constructing two opposing injections and contrast equalities with Cantor's strict inequality |A| < |P(A)|. Leaves cardinal arithmetic, the Continuum Hypothesis, and ZFC ordinal/cardinal theory to advanced set theory.

nodes.label: Canonical Factorization of Functions Through Quotient Sets
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment synthesizing partitions and quotient sets with function composition and bijections to unify equivalence relations and mappings. Defines the kernel equivalence relation (fibers) of any function f : A → B by x ∼_f y ⇔ f(x) = f(y) and verifies that its equivalence classes are the nonempty preimages f^{-1}({y}) for y ∈ im(f). Proves the universal property of the canonical quotient map π : A → A/∼ (a function g : A → C factors uniquely through π as g = ḡ ∘ π iff x ∼ y ⇒ g(x) = g(y)) and derives the Canonical Factorization Theorem (Set-Theoretic First Isomorphism Theorem): every function f : A → B factors uniquely as f = ι ∘ f̄ ∘ π, where π : A → A/∼_f is surjective, f̄ : A/∼_f → im(f) is bijective, and ι : im(f) ↪ B is the injective inclusion map. Applies this factorization to concrete maps (such as modular projection and trigonometric/squaring maps) to preview quotient isomorphism theorems in abstract algebra and topology.

nodes.label: Order-Preserving Maps, Order Isomorphisms, and Lattices
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment synthesizing poset bounds and suprema with injectivity, surjectivity, and bijections to compare ordered structures. Defines order-preserving (monotone) maps, order embeddings (x ≤ y ⇔ f(x) ≤ f(y)), and order isomorphisms (bijective order embeddings), explicitly proving via a concrete finite poset counterexample that a bijective order-preserving map need not be an order isomorphism unless its inverse is also order-preserving (whereas on total orders, every bijective monotone map is an order isomorphism). Introduces lattices as posets in which every pair of elements has a join (supremum) and meet (infimum), verifies core examples ((P(X), ⊆), (ℤ^+, |), and any total order), and shows that order isomorphisms preserve minimal/maximal elements, bounds, joins, and meets. Enables the learner to distinguish isomorphism classes of small posets and test lattice structure without entering Boolean algebra representation theory.
